claims.text: Training reinforcement-learning policies over many environment variations can be inefficient and plateau at suboptimal performance.

GSL trains a generalist until a performance plateau, initializes specialists from its checkpoint on disjoint subsets of the lowest-performing variations, and resumes generalist training using demonstrations from specialists and from the generalist on remaining variations.
The experiments combine PPO or PPG with DAPG on Procgen, PPO with DAPG on Meta-World, and SAC with GAIL on ManiSkill, including online environment interactions during demonstration-guided learning.
Procgen evaluation uses seven selected challenging environments, with 1024 training levels and 1000 unseen test levels per environment; reported results average five runs with standard deviations.
Meta-World experiments use V2 MT-10 and MT-50, containing 10 and 50 skills respectively, and evaluate performance only on training environments.
On BigFish, PPO-based GSL achieves training return 31.1±0.8 versus PPO's 24.6±0.7, and test return 30.0±0.5 versus 24.3±1.1; these are raw episode reward means and standard deviations over five runs.
Meta-World training success rates increase from 58.4±10.1% to 77.5±2.9% on MT-10 and from 31.1±4.5% to 43.5±2.2% on MT-50, averaged over five runs.

In timing ablations on BigFish and PushChair, launching specialists before the generalist plateau worsens sample complexity; training specialists from scratch is reported as inefficient and ineffective.
On BigFish, GSL with behavior cloning obtains training/test returns of 25.3±0.4/22.1±0.9, compared with 31.1±0.8/30.0±0.5 for GSL with DAPG and 24.6±0.7/24.3±1.1 for PPO alone.

ManiSkill evaluation is restricted to a reduced PushChair setup with eight chairs because physical simulation and point-cloud rendering are expensive, with an observed speed of 30 environment steps per second.

The plateau criterion requires hyperparameter tuning: starting too early loses initial generalist efficiency, while starting too late wastes samples and could make specialist-guided fine-tuning harder.
The DnC RL comparison was skipped because the authors found its quadratic computational complexity in the number of specialists computationally intractable in their setup.
The paper contributes a generalist-specialist meta-algorithm integrating reinforcement learning with learning from demonstrations, and identifies specialist-training timing as a key design choice.
